passages.english: Homer said that one mourns a dead man with the belly;
passages.notes: Single verse without context. It alludes to Iliad 19.225, where Odysseus says the Achaeans should not mourn a corpse by fasting (γαστέρι).

passages.original: τὴν Κίρκην οὔ φημι, καθὼς εἴρηκεν Ὅμηρος,
passages.english: I do not say that Circe, as Homer has said,

passages.original: ὁ φθόνος οἰκτιρμοῦ, κατὰ Πίνδαρον, ἐστιν ἀμείνων
passages.english: Envy, according to Pindar, is better than pity.

passages.original: οὐδʼ ὅσα τὰς Θήβας εἶπεν Ὅμηρος ἔχειν
passages.english: nor as many as Homer said Thebes held
passages.notes: Single verse without context. It probably alludes to the wealth or the hundred gates of Egyptian Thebes (Iliad 9.381–384).

passages.original: ὅττι μένος μερόπων οἶνον Ὅμηρος ἔφη.
passages.english: because Homer called wine the strength of mortals.
passages.notes: Single verse without context. μερόπων is the Homeric epithet for mortals or men. The allusion is to Iliad 6.261 on wine and strength (μένος).

passages.original: ἐξ ἀτόμων Ἐπίκουρος ὅλον τὸν κόσμον ἔγραψεν
passages.english: Epicurus wrote that the whole world [is] made of atoms

passages.original: οὔτε Χίμαιρα τοιοῦτον ἔπνει κακὸν ἡ καθʼ Ὅμηρον
passages.english: Not even the Chimaera in Homer breathed such evil
passages.notes: Single verse, incomplete without context. The allusion is to the fire-breathing Chimaera of Iliad 6.182.

passages.original: κεῖθι τὸ νημερτὲς γνώσεαι ὡς ὁ Πλάτων.
passages.english: there you will know the unerring truth, as Plato [did].
passages.notes: Single verse without context. The comparison 'as Plato' is elliptical. It may mean 'as Plato says' or 'like Plato'.

passages.original: ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, καθὼς εἴρηκεν Ἄρατος·
passages.english: Let us begin from Zeus, as Aratus has said;
passages.notes: Single verse. It quotes the opening of Aratus' Phaenomena.
